Pairs share proteins across splits; I'll run the overlap check with a per-protein baseline.I couldn't write a Results paragraph that supports the generalization claim, because a baseline with no sequence information matches PairNet's AUROC. So below is a paragraph that reports what the data show, plus the numbers behind it.

**Draft Results paragraph**

> On 140 held-out protein pairs (random 80/20 split of 700 tested pairs over 60 yeast proteins; 22.9% positives in test), PairNet achieved an AUROC of 0.79. However, every test pair consisted of two proteins that also appeared in the training set (all 60 proteins occur in both splits), so the split measures generalization to new pairings of already-seen proteins, not to new proteins. A baseline that uses no sequence information, scoring each test pair by the mean training interaction rate of its two proteins, reached an AUROC of 0.79 (0.795), indistinguishable from PairNet. The test performance is therefore explained by per-protein interaction propensity (e.g. promiscuous versus non-interacting proteins) and provides no evidence that PairNet has learned sequence determinants of interaction or that it will generalize to uncharacterized proteins.

**Numbers**
- PairNet test AUROC: 0.790 (n = 140).
- Per-protein label-rate baseline AUROC: 0.795.
- Test proteins not seen in training: 0 of 60. Test pairs with both proteins seen in training: 100%. Exact pair duplicates between train and test: 0.
- Positive rate: 17.9% in train, 22.9% in test.

**What this means for the claim**
- The claim that PairNet generalizes to uncharacterized proteins is untested by this split. It also looks unsupported, since the baseline explains the score.
- To test it, re-split so that test proteins never appear in training (the strict version, with both proteins held out, is the closest match to uncharacterized proteins). Then report PairNet against the per-protein baseline.
- I only had the predictions, not the embeddings, so I couldn't re-run the model on a protein-disjoint split. If you share them, I can set that up.
- I'd drop or soften the "learned sequence determinants" wording until that result is in.

import pandas as pd,numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score as auc
tr=pd.read_csv('pairs_train.csv');te=pd.read_csv('pairs_test.csv');p=pd.read_csv('predictions_test.csv')
m=te.merge(p,on=['protein_a','protein_b']);print(len(te),len(m),auc(m.label,m.score))
S=lambda d:set(d.protein_a)|set(d.protein_b)
print(len(S(tr)),len(S(te)),len(S(te)-S(tr)))
print('both seen',np.mean([(a in S(tr)) and (b in S(tr)) for a,b in zip(te.protein_a,te.protein_b)]))
print('pairs dup',len(set(zip(te.protein_a,te.protein_b))&set(zip(tr.protein_a,tr.protein_b))))

# per-protein label rate baseline
l=pd.concat([tr.rename(columns={'protein_a':'p'})[['p','label']],tr.rename(columns={'protein_b':'p'})[['p','label']]])
r=l.groupby('p').label.mean();g=tr.label.mean()
s=[(r.get(a,g)+r.get(b,g))/2 for a,b in zip(te.protein_a,te.protein_b)]
print('baseline',auc(te.label,s))
